Acrylic paint-along · beginner

A small red sailboat with a white sail on teal water at sunset

Start on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

17 stepsCanvas: 16 x 12 inFocal point: the white sail against the orange sky Light: the low sun just above the horizon, in the middle of the picture, behind and to the left of the boatHow this lesson was made

Get these out of the box before you start. Every paint in the lesson is mixed from them; squeeze out a little of each when its step comes up.

  • Titanium whitefirst in step 1
  • Cadmium yellow medium (hue)first in step 1
  • Cadmium red medium (hue)first in step 1
  • Ultramarine bluefirst in step 1
  • Burnt siennafirst in step 3

What you need

Brushes

  • 1 inch wide flat: Blend the sunset sky, violet to orangeFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • #6 round: Paint the sunRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • 3/4 inch flat: Lay in the far hillFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • 1 inch flat: Lay in the teal waterFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • 1/2 inch flat (on its edge): Lay the first layer of the sun pathFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • 1/2 inch flat: Block in the red hullFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • 1/4 inch flat: Shade the right half of the hullFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • liner: Light the hull's top rimLiner: long, very thin bristles, for fine lines like twigs and grass

Also

  • A 16 x 12 in canvas, landscape (hang it that way). Using another size? Scale every measurement.
  • A ruler
  • Water jar and paper towel
  • Palette or paper plate for mixing

You don't have to mix them all at the start: each step lists the paints it uses with their recipes, so you can mix a little as you go before it dries. Parts are by volume.

Before you start

Placing shapes with a transfer outline optional

The transfer outline (optional)

The outlines of the main shapes, on a grid of quarters: 1 Red hull; 2 White sails. On your 16 x 12 in canvas the grid lines are 4 in apart across and 3 in apart down. Before the stage that starts one, you can lightly chalk its outline on the canvas, measuring from the edges with a ruler.

Strokes to try on scrap paper first

Each one's card is open in the step that first uses it.

  • Side-to-side blend, first in step 1.
  • Small circles, first in step 2.
  • Horizontal strokes, first in step 3.
  • Horizontal dashes, first in step 7.
  • Building from pieces, first in step 9.
  • Curved strokes, first in step 10.
  • Liner work, first in step 11. Try a few lines on scrap paper first.
  • Pull-down, first in step 15.

The basics

Before you start not checked yet

Before you start

Not checked yet

  • Two water jars: one to rinse the brush, one kept clean for thinning paint. A big clear jar shows when the rinse water is dirty.
  • A rag or paper towel, to wipe the brush between colors.
  • Put out bigger puddles of paint than you think you need. Big puddles stay wet longer than small smears.
  • Lay your colors out the same way every time, so they're easy to find and don't get dragged into each other.
Keep your colors clean not checked yet

Keep your colors clean

Not checked yet

  • Wipe the brush on a rag between colors.
  • Rinse it fully before going into white.
  • Rinse often. Dirty water tints every color with the last one.
  • Mix on the palette, not on the canvas. Two or three colors at most: stop when the color is right.
Colors dry darker not checked yet

Colors dry darker

Not checked yet

  • Acrylic looks lighter when wet than when dry.
  • Before a big area, paint a test swatch and let it dry before judging the mix.
Fixing a mistake not checked yet

Fixing a mistake

Not checked yet

  • Acrylic is forgiving. Let the area dry, then paint over it and try again.
  • Don't keep working a spot that's half dry. Leave it, work somewhere else, and come back.
Keep paint from drying on the palette not checked yet

Keep paint from drying on the palette

Not checked yet

  • Acrylic on a brushstroke stays wet for only a few minutes.
  • Mist the palette lightly with a spray bottle now and then. Only lightly: too much water weakens the paint.
  • Cover the paint when you aren't using it.
Let each layer dry not checked yet

Let each layer dry

Not checked yet

  • Between steps, the paint underneath should be dry to the touch. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  • Painting into half-dry paint drags it up and turns it gooey and muddy.
  • Thick paint can feel dry on top and still be wet inside. Give thick areas longer.
  • Fine lines and light colors over dark especially need a dry layer underneath.
Light colors over dark need more than one coat not checked yet

Light colors over dark need more than one coat

Not checked yet

  • One coat of white or a light color over a dark one usually looks gray and patchy.
  • Expect two or three thin coats, letting each dry. Use the paint thick, with little water.
Making a color lighter or darker not checked yet

Making a color lighter or darker

Not checked yet

  • To lighten: add the color to the white a little at a time, not white to the color.
  • White also dulls a color. Too much turns it chalky.
  • To darken: add the dark into the lighter mix in small amounts.
  • For the next lighter value of something, start from the mix you already have and add white, so the colors stay related.
One light direction not checked yet

One light direction

Not checked yet

  • Pick where the light comes from and put every highlight on that side.
  • Each thing is built the same way: the whole shape in a darker or middle value, a lighter value on the side facing the light, then the lightest on a small area at the very edge. Each covers less than the one before.
The ugly stage not checked yet

The ugly stage

Not checked yet

  • Partway through, every painting looks flat or wrong. That's normal. Keep building.
  • Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.
  • Details come last, and only on shapes that are already right.
How much water not checked yet

How much water

Not checked yet

  • Keep water to about half the mix or less. More than that makes weak, see-through color that can lift when you paint over it.
  • For covering, use the paint thick, with little or no water.
  • After rinsing, wipe the metal part of the brush dry.

The sunset sky 2 steps

STEP 1 OF 17 · The sunset sky, 1 of 2

Blend the sunset sky, violet to orange

  1. Inside the outlined area, all the way across from the top edge, down to about 5 in from the bottom edge, a little below where the hill's base and the water will go.
  2. Paints, top to bottom: Twilight violet across the top, Sunset coral in the band below it, then Sunset orange down past the horizon.
  3. Brush: 1 inch wide flat. Load: An even coat, neither thick nor thin.
  4. Start with the darkest color and stroke side to side. Without rinsing, pick up the next lighter color and paint below it. Then stroke back up over the join several times.
  5. It should leave smooth bands of color, with a soft join where two wet colors meet.
  6. Watch out: Blending after the paint has started to drag. Acrylic sets in minutes, and scrubbing setting paint lifts it and leaves streaks. Fix: stop as soon as it drags.
  7. Let it dry, then blend a new thin layer on top.

Tip: The light is the low sun just above the horizon, a little left of the middle, so the sky is brightest and most orange around it. Run the orange on below the hill line; the hill and water go over it.

Stroke: Side-to-side blend how to do it, not checked yet

Side-to-side blend

Not checked yet

With. wide flat; 3/4 inch wash brush

Load. An even coat, neither thick nor thin.

Motion. Start with the darkest color and stroke side to side. Without rinsing, pick up the next lighter color and paint below it. Then stroke back up over the join several times.

What it leaves. Smooth bands of color, with a soft join where two wet colors meet.

Then. Stroke back over each join while it's wet.

Blend two colors side to side

Dashed outline: what to paint in that picture. Arrows: which way to move the brush.

If it goes wrong.

  • A hard line where two colors meet. Add more of the lighter color at the join and blend again.
  • Two very different colors won't blend. Mix a bridge color from the two on the palette (pink and yellow make orange) and paint it between them.
  • The brush is overloaded. Wipe it on a rag. Rinse before going into white.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 2 OF 17 · The sunset sky, 2 of 2

Paint the sun

  1. Let the sunset sky dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Rinse the brush fully first: this is the lightest paint yet.
  3. Inside the outlined area. Its top is about 4 1/2 in from the top edge, and its left side is about 7 in from the left edge; it's about 1 in wide and 1 in tall.
  4. Paint: Pale sun yellow.
  5. Brush: #6 round.
  6. Fill the circle with small circles of the brush tip, working from the middle outward, so the edge stays soft and round.
  7. It should leave a round, soft-edged disk with a slightly bumpy rim.
  8. Watch out: The edge is too hard. Fix: soften it with lighter passes of the same small circles.
  9. Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.

Tip: The sun sits a little left of the middle, about 1/2 in above the far shore line, as the Where picture shows. Keep it a clean circle; it's the brightest thing in the sky.

Small circles

Not checked yet

Motion. Small circles with the tip of the brush make a cloud's bumpy top edge. Around a sun or moon, circular strokes move outward from it.

What it leaves. A bumpy, soft edge.

Then. Smooth with the same circular motion, and highlight only the lit top edges.

Little circles along the top

Dashed outline: what to paint in that picture. Arrows: which way to move the brush.

If it goes wrong.

  • The edge is too hard. Soften it with lighter passes. On a cloud, smudging with a finger works too.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

The far hill and shore 2 steps

STEP 3 OF 17 · The far hill and shore, 1 of 2

Lay in the far hill

  1. Let the sunset sky dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Rinse the brush well first. Dirty water tints every color with the last one.
  3. Inside the outlined area. Its top is about 4 1/2 in from the top edge, and its left side is at the left edge; it's about 14 1/2 in wide and 2 in tall.
  4. Paint: Dusk purple.
  5. Mix enough Dusk purple for this step and step 4; cover it between them.
  6. Brush: 3/4 inch flat.
  7. Keep the brush level and the strokes long, left and right.
  8. It should leave a flat, solid purple hill with slight level streaks that follow the stroke, and no texture.

Tip: The hill rises from the left edge to its rounded top about 2 in in, then slopes gently down to the right into a low band that runs on along the horizon almost to the right edge. Keep it flat and soft: it's far away, so no texture.

STEP 4 OF 17 · The far hill and shore, 2 of 2

Lay in the shore behind the boat

  1. Let the far hill and shore, and the sunset sky dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. A thin band along the horizon, from where the hill ends to the right edge, behind where the boat will go. Its top is about 6 in from the top edge, and it's about 1/2 in tall.
  3. Paint: Dusk purple.
  4. Brush: 3/4 inch flat.
  5. Keep the brush level and the strokes long, left and right.
  6. It should leave one thin, level purple band along the horizon, with slight streaks that follow the stroke.
  7. Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.

Tip: This is the same purple as the hill, in one thin level band. Keep its top edge straight and level, and run it on behind where the boat will go.

The water 2 steps

STEP 5 OF 17 · The water, 1 of 2

Lay in the teal water

  1. Let the far hill and shore, and the sunset sky dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area, all the way across to the bottom edge. Its top is about 6 1/2 in from the top edge, right under the shore band.
  3. Paint: Deep teal.
  4. Mix enough Deep teal for this step and step 14; cover it between them.
  5. Brush: 1 inch flat.
  6. Keep the brush level and the strokes long, left and right.
  7. It should leave flat, level bands of teal that read as water stretching away, with slight streaks that follow the stroke.

Tip: Paint straight over where the sun path and the boat's reflection will go; they go on top later. Keep every stroke level so the water lies flat.

STEP 6 OF 17 · The water, 2 of 2

Streak in the lighter water

  1. Let the teal water, and the far hill and shore dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area, all the way across to the bottom edge. Its top is about 5 1/2 in from the bottom edge.
  3. Paint: Soft teal.
  4. Brush: 3/4 inch flat.
  5. Keep the brush level and the strokes long, left and right.
  6. It should leave thin, level streaks of lighter teal that read as water stretching away.
  7. Leave what step 5 painted showing around these marks, as in the Result picture.
  8. Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.

Tip: Keep the streaks thin and close together near the horizon and longer and farther apart toward the bottom. Leave plenty of the deep teal showing between them. A few streaks on the left pick up a faint warm glint from the sky; keep those few and small.

The sun path 2 steps

STEP 7 OF 17 · The sun path, 1 of 2

Lay the first layer of the sun path

  1. Let the water, and the far hill and shore dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area. Its bottom is about 3/4 in from the bottom edge, and its left side is about 1 3/4 in from the left edge; it's about 10 in wide and 5 in tall.
  3. Paint: Dull gold.
  4. Brush: 1/2 inch flat (on its edge). Load: Creamy paint, a light touch.
  5. Short, level dashes. Small and close together near the horizon, longer and wider apart lower down.
  6. It should leave short, flat, level marks with gaps of the water color between them.
  7. Watch out: The dashes smear into the water. The water underneath is still wet. Fix: paint them over dry water only.

Tip: The path runs straight down from under the sun, narrow at the horizon and wider toward the bottom. Make it a column of separate level dashes, not one solid stripe.

Brighten the middle of the sun path

  1. Let the sun path on the water and the water dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area. Its bottom is about 3/4 in from the bottom edge, and its left side is about 2 in from the left edge; it's about 8 1/2 in wide and 5 in tall.

The sailboat 6 steps

STEP 9 OF 17 · The sailboat, 1 of 6

Block in the red hull

  1. Let the water, and the far hill and shore dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Optional: lightly chalk its outline first, from the transfer outline in Before you start, measuring from the canvas edges with a ruler.
  3. Inside the outlined area. Its bottom is about 4 in from the bottom edge, and its right side is about 1 1/4 in from the right edge; it's about 3 1/2 in wide and 1 in tall.
  4. Paint: Boat red.
  5. Brush: 1/2 inch flat.
  6. Start with one long, shallow curved piece for the body of the hull, flat on top and rounded underneath. Then add the pointed bow on the right and the squarer stern on the left as smaller pieces.
  7. It should leave one solid red hull shape. Soften where the pieces meet so it reads as one boat.

Tip: The hull is a long, shallow boat shape about 3 1/2 in long and under 1 in deep, its bottom about 4 in up from the bottom edge, as the Where picture shows. The pointed bow is on the right and lifts a little; the stern on the left is squarer. Carry the red a little below the hull's bottom edge into the water: that thin strip is the start of its reflection.

Stroke: Building from pieces how to do it, not checked yet

Building from pieces

Not checked yet

Motion. Start with one simple shape (an oval, a circle, or a rectangle). Then add the rest in curved pieces on each side, like ( ), smaller toward the edges.

What it leaves. A shape made of distinct curved segments with small gaps or overlaps between them.

Then. Soften where the pieces meet only if the picture shows smooth ribs; otherwise leave the segments visible.

STEP 10 OF 17 · The sailboat, 2 of 6

Shade the right half of the hull

  1. Let the red hull and the water dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area. Its bottom is about 4 in from the bottom edge, and its right side is about 1 1/2 in from the right edge; it's about 3 in wide and 1 in tall.
  3. Paint: Shadow red.
  4. Brush: 1/4 inch flat.
  5. Bend each stroke with the hull's shape: follow its curve from the middle out to the pointed bow, the way the planks run.
  6. It should leave darker red marks that bend with the hull, which is what makes it look rounded.
  7. Leave what step 9 painted showing around these marks, as in the Result picture.

Tip: The sun is behind the boat on the left, so the right half of the hull, toward the bow, is in shade. Keep the left end bright red, and carry the darker red along the strip just under the hull too.

STEP 15 OF 17 · The boat's reflection, 1 of 3

Pull down the hull's reflection

  1. Let the sailboat and the water dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area. Its bottom is about 1/2 in from the bottom edge, and its right side is about 1 1/2 in from the right edge; it's about 3 1/2 in wide and 5 in tall.
  3. Paint: Dark rust.
  4. Brush: 1/2 inch flat. Load: Load the brush, then wipe it until only a little paint is left.
  5. Stroke straight down, starting just below the hull, in short strokes that break up as they go down.
  6. It should leave soft, streaky, see-through dark red strokes right under the hull, not a sharp copy of it.
  7. Watch out: The reflection as sharp and detailed as the object. It looks like a mirror or a second picture. Fix: fewer details, softer edges, a thin dry brush.

Tip: Start right under the hull and keep the strokes as wide as the boat, in a thin band about 1/2 in tall. The reflection is softer and a little darker than the hull; let it break up into short strokes.

How this lesson was made

You don't need any of this to paint. It's for the curious: how Claude read your photo, picked a technique, and chose between free filters and paid image renders for every picture above.

Numbers are steps. Every step is cut from the one finished painting, inside the outline of the part it paints, so no step picture was rendered.

How Claude read your photosubject, light, layers

Before starting

Subject: A red sailboat with a white sail on teal water at sunset, with an orange and purple sky, a low sun with its path on the water, and a purple hill on the left.

Found in the image: just the picture

Done: none

Why: No bars, borders, captions, or scene around the picture; the whole image is the painting.

Fitted to your canvas

Canvas: 16 x 12 in, landscape (default, no --canvas)

Done: crop

Left out: about 5.6% of the frame's width off each side (empty sky, hill tip on the left, empty water on the right)

Why: fit-canvas picked 12x16 as the standard size closest to the photo's 3:2 shape; the 4:3 canvas sits inside the 3:2 frame with a strip off each side, keeping the boat, its reflection, the sun, and the sun path whole. No render needed.

Beginner version

What made it too busy: No tiny separate things besides the boat, which is the subject. No texture made of hundreds of items: the ripples and the sun path are rows of level dashes, one repeated mark. No detail inside big shapes beyond loose horizontal sky strokes. About 8 parts, within max_parts for a 192 sq in canvas.

Why: Every answer in step 0c is no, so the lesson is made from the photo itself.

A calm sunset seascape: a violet-to-orange sky, a low sun with its golden path on teal water, a purple hill on the left, and a small red sailboat with white sails on the right. The boat is the subject; the hard parts for a beginner are keeping the water's dashes level and the reflection soft and broken. The lesson is about painting back to front and letting each layer dry before the dashes and reflection go on.

Subject: A small red sailboat with a white sail on teal water at sunset
Focal point: the white sail against the orange sky
Light: the low sun just above the horizon, in the middle of the picture, behind and to the left of the boat

What it saw, back to front

  1. Sunset sky
  2. Far hill and shore
  3. Far shore behind the boat
  4. Teal water
  5. Red hull
  6. White sails
  7. Mast and boom
Why this techniquePaint along, back to front
ChosenPaint along, back to frontStart on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

A simple sunset seascape for a beginner: a sky gradient, a far hill, water, and one boat, painted back to front on a white canvas the way paint-along sailboat sunsets are taught. It's also the only approach with version 2 keys.

Passed onBlock in, then build up (acrylic-block-in-beginner.yaml)

Kept as an option, but beginner acrylic lessons use paint-along (docs/decisions.md), and it has no version 2 keys.

How the paint recipes were worked out15 paints, free

Paint doesn't mix like light on a screen: blue and yellow make green, not gray. So the recipes come from a pigment mixing model (Mixbox), not a guess. For each paint it tried every simple recipe from your tubes, up to three colors plus white, and kept the one that lands closest to the color in the painting. Delta E is how far off it lands: under 2 is hard to see, under 5 is close, and over 8 means these tubes can't quite make it.

Why the steps go in this order17 steps

Back to front: the sky first, run past the horizon, then the sun on it; the far hill and shore; the water over the sky's lower edge; the sun path on the dry water; then the boat (hull, sails, mast); and the reflection last, once everything above the water is dry, as the technique's water rule says.

  1. 1. Blend the sunset sky, violet to orange

    The farthest thing, blended wet in one go, run past the horizon so the hill and water go over it.

  2. 2. Paint the sun

    Sits on the dry sky; one small shape before anything in front of it.

  3. 3. Lay in the far hill

    The farthest land, painted over the dry sky.

  4. 4. Lay in the shore behind the boat

    The same shore band, carried on to the right edge behind where the boat goes.

  5. 5. Lay in the teal water

    The water's base coat goes on once everything above it is dry, straight over where the path and reflection will go.

  6. 6. Streak in the lighter water

    The lighter streaks give the water its surface before anything sits on it.

  7. 7. Lay the first layer of the sun path

    The sun path's first layer, on dry water, in the darker gold so the brighter middle can go on top.

  8. 8. Brighten the middle of the sun path

    The brightest dashes, smaller than the first layer, after it's dry.

  9. 9. Block in the red hull

    The boat sits in front of the water, so it goes on after the water and path; its hull first, the biggest piece.

  10. 10. Shade the right half of the hull

    The hull's shaded side, away from the sun, over the dry base.

  11. 11. Light the hull's top rim

    The hull's lightest accent last, a thin rim on the top edge.

  12. 12. Block in the white sails

    The sails stand above the hull; painted after it so their bases sit right on the deck.

  13. 13. Line in the mast and boom

    A liner line over the dry sails and hull.

  14. 14. Catch the light on the mast

    The thin teal line under the boom, over the dry dark line.

  15. 15. Pull down the hull's reflection

    Reflections go on once everything above the water is dry; the hull's red first, right under it.

  16. 16. Pull down the sail's shadow reflection

    The sails' darker reflection, below the red.

  17. 17. Pull down the sail's light

    The lightest part of the reflection last, leaving the darker strokes showing.

What the reviewer caught8 notes

A second Claude, with fresh eyes and none of this reasoning, compared each picture with its neighbors and the finish. It gets two rounds of fixes, then stops; anything still off is flagged on its step. A third checked each step's words against a measured map of what the picture changed, asking whether a beginner following them would get there.

  • Text check: vague Step 3: x 45-90, y 50-56: the purple band runs on along the horizon almost to the right edge, but the tip said the hill flattens into the shore before the middle (fixed)
  • Text check: missing Step 4: x 90-92, y 62-65: a navy dot appears on bare canvas below the horizon; no line paints it, and step 5's water covers it (left: a cut artifact of the step picture (a navy dot below the horizon on bare canvas); the water in the next step paints over it, and the text can't fix a picture)
  • Text check: vague Step 5: x 0-100, y 54: the water's top edge sits at about 6 1/2 in from the top, but the Where line said about 5 in (fixed)

  • Text check: wrong_result Step 14: x 72-89, y 57-59: only the boom changes; the mast stays dark, but the tip said taupe runs down most of the mast (fixed)

What Claude would do differentlyfor the next lesson
  • The far hill's outline wouldn't take the shore band right of the boat (points_in there did nothing), so that band became its own area part, far-shore, with the same paint.
  • The reflection's outline missed the mast's dark zigzag and its bottom tip until it got measured colors_in/colors_out from part-colors; its points alone didn't move it.
  • The hull's outline always takes a thin strip of its own red reflection just under the waterline, and a box tight enough to leave it gives the hull's bottom edge to the sky. Kept the loose-box version and told the painter the strip is the start of the reflection.
  • A tool artifact: step 4 (far-shore) shows a navy dot below the horizon on bare canvas, at the hull's lower right corner. No part owns it; the next step's water covers it. Recorded under Known problems.
